name: On-Chain Forensics
title: On-Chain Forensics
answer: On-chain forensics is the practice of tracing activity on public blockchains to identify who moved what, when, and why. It covers illicit finance, sanctions evasion, exchange hacks, ransomware payments, fraud, and market manipulation. It also supports compliance work at exchanges, custodians, and DeFi protocols, where teams need to screen wallets and explain transaction histories. The field sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, and it borrows methods from graph analysis, data engineering, and machine learning.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: On-chain forensics is the practice of tracing activity on public blockchains to identify who moved what, when, and why. It covers illicit finance, sanctions evasion, exchange hacks, ransomware payments, fraud, and market manipulation. It also supports compliance work at exchanges, custodians, and DeFi protocols, where teams need to screen wallets and explain transaction histories. The field sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, and it borrows methods from graph analysis, data engineering, and machine learning.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on blockchain nodes, archive nodes, and indexers that provide raw transaction and state data. Teams store that data in graph databases and data warehouses, then use APIs from commercial analytics platforms and open-source tools to query address clusters and entity labels. AI models handle clustering, anomaly detection, and risk scoring, while cloud compute and stream processing support near real-time monitoring. Because chains differ in their data models, the infrastructure often includes cross-chain bridges and protocol-specific decoders.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start by collecting transaction data from nodes and indexers, then build a graph of addresses, transactions, and smart contract interactions. Heuristics and machine learning group addresses that likely belong to the same entity, and manual review confirms or rejects those clusters. Investigators trace flows through mixers, bridges, and DeFi protocols, often using time analysis and counterparty patterns to follow funds across chains. Risk scoring then flags wallets for sanctions, fraud, or money laundering exposure, and the findings are written into reports for exchanges, law enforcement, or courts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: On-chain forensics raises questions about privacy, data protection, and the legal weight of blockchain evidence. Analysts must handle personal data carefully, especially when wallet clusters are linked to real identities, and they need clear provenance for every label and risk score. Chain of custody, audit trails, and reproducible methods matter when findings are used in regulatory filings or legal proceedings. False positives can freeze funds or damage reputations, so governance covers review processes, appeals, and jurisdiction-specific rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward cross-chain tracing, real-time monitoring, and tighter integration with traditional finance compliance. Privacy coins, zero-knowledge proofs, and layer two networks create new gaps that analysts and tool builders are trying to close. AI is likely to take on more of the clustering and anomaly detection work, while human analysts focus on attribution and reporting. Regulators are also pushing for standardised data formats and clearer rules on what counts as admissible evidence.
